vsm1.3:95.1: By the kind of states occurring:
vsm1.3:95.2: in one of greedy temperament there is frequent occurrence of such states as deceit, fraud, pride, evilness of wishes,
vsm1.3:95.3: greatness of wishes, discontent, foppery and personal vanity.
vsm1.3:95.4: In one of hating temperament there is frequent occurrence of such states as anger, enmity, disparaging, domineering,
vsm1.3:95.6: In one of deluded temperament there is frequent occurrence of such states as stiffness, torpor, agitation, worry,
vsm1.3:95.7: uncertainty, and holding on tenaciously with refusal to relinquish.
vsm1.3:95.8:
In one of faithful temperament there is frequent occurrence of such states as free generosity,
desire to see Noble Ones, desire to hear the Good Dhamma,
vsm1.3:95.9: great gladness, ingenuousness, honesty, and trust in things that inspire trust.
vsm1.3:95.10:
In one of intelligent temperament there is frequent occurrence of such states
as readiness to be spoken to, possession of good friends, knowledge of the right amount in eating,
vsm1.3:95.11: mindfulness and full awareness, devotion to wakefulness,
vsm1.3:95.12: a sense of urgency about things that should inspire a sense of urgency, and wisely directed endeavour.
vsm1.3:95.13:
In one of speculative temperament there is frequent occurrence of such states as talkativeness,
sociability, boredom with devotion to the profitable,
vsm1.3:95.15: smoking by night and flaming by day (see M I 144—that is to say, hatching plans at night and putting them into effect by day),
vsm1.3:95.16: and mental running hither and thither (see Ud 37).
vsm1.3:95.17: This is how the temperaments may be recognized by the kind of states occurring.
vsm1.3:96.1:
However, these directions for recognizing the temperaments have not been handed
down in their entirety in either the texts or the commentaries;
vsm1.3:96.2: they are only expressed according to the opinion of the teachers
vsm1.3:96.3: and cannot therefore be treated as authentic.
vsm1.3:96.4: For even those of hating temperament can exhibit postures, etc., ascribed to the greedy temperament when they try diligently.
vsm1.3:96.5: And postures, etc., never arise with distinct characteristics in a person of mixed temperament.
vsm1.3:96.6: Only such directions for recognizing temperament as are given in the commentaries should be treated as authentic;
vsm1.3:96.8: “A teacher who has acquired penetration of minds will know the temperament and will explain a meditation subject accordingly;
vsm1.3:96.9: one who has not should question the pupil.”
vsm1.3:96.10: So it is by penetration of minds or by questioning the person, that it can be known
vsm1.3:96.11: whether he is one of greedy temperament
vsm1.3:96.12: or one of those beginning with hating temperament.
vsm1.3:97.1: What suits one of what kind of temperament? (§79).
vsm1.3:97.2: A suitable lodging for one of greedy temperament
vsm1.3:97.3: has an unwashed sill and stands level with the ground,
vsm1.3:97.4: and it can be either an overhanging rock with an unprepared drip-ledge (see Ch. II, note 15), a grass hut, or a leaf house, etc.
vsm1.3:97.5: It ought to be spattered with dirt, full of bats, dilapidated,
vsm1.3:97.6: too high or too low, in bleak surroundings, threatened by lions, tigers, etc., with a muddy, uneven path,
vsm1.3:97.7: where even the bed and chair are full of bugs.
vsm1.3:97.8: And it should be ugly and unsightly, exciting loathing as soon as looked at.
vsm1.3:97.9: Suitable inner and outer garments are those that have torn-off edges with threads hanging down all round like a “net cake,”
vsm1.3:97.10: harsh to the touch like hemp,
vsm1.3:97.11: soiled, heavy and hard to wear.
vsm1.3:97.12: And the right kind of bowl for him is an ugly clay bowl
vsm1.3:97.13: disfigured by stoppings and joints, or a heavy and misshapen iron bowl as unappetizing as a skull.
vsm1.3:97.14: The right kind of road for him on which to wander for alms is disagreeable, with no village near, and uneven.
vsm1.3:97.15: The right kind of village for him in which to wander for alms is where people wander about as if oblivious of him,
vsm1.3:97.16:
where, as he is about to leave without getting alms even from a single family,
people call him into the sitting hall, saying, “Come, venerable sir,”
vsm1.3:97.17: and give him gruel and rice,
vsm1.3:97.18: but do so as casually as if they were putting a cow in a pen.
vsm1.3:97.19: Suitable people to serve him are slaves or workmen
vsm1.3:97.20: who are unsightly, ill-favoured, with dirty clothes, ill-smelling and disgusting,
vsm1.3:97.21: who serve him his gruel and rice as if they were throwing it rudely at him.
vsm1.3:97.22: The right kind of gruel and rice and hard food is poor, unsightly,
vsm1.3:97.23: made up of millet, kudusaka, broken rice, etc.,
vsm1.3:97.24: stale buttermilk, sour gruel, curry of old vegetables,
vsm1.3:97.25: or anything at all that is merely for filling the stomach.
vsm1.3:97.26: The right kind of posture for him is either standing or walking.
vsm1.3:97.27: The object of his contemplation should be any of the colour kasiṇas, beginning with the blue, whose colour is not pure.
vsm1.3:97.28: This is what suits one of greedy temperament.
vsm1.3:98.1: A suitable resting place for one of hating temperament
vsm1.3:98.2: is not too high or too low,
vsm1.3:98.4: with well-proportioned walls, posts and steps,
vsm1.3:98.5: with well-prepared frieze work and lattice work, brightened with various kinds of painting, with an even, smooth, soft floor,
vsm1.3:98.6: adorned with festoons of flowers and a canopy of many-coloured cloth like a Brahmā-god’s divine palace,
vsm1.3:98.7: with bed and chair covered with well-spread clean pretty covers,
vsm1.3:98.8: smelling sweetly of flowers, and perfumes and scents set about for homely comfort,
vsm1.3:98.9: which makes one happy and glad at the mere sight of it.
vsm1.3:99.1: The right kind of road to his lodging is free from any sort of danger,
vsm1.3:99.4:
And here it is best that the lodging’s furnishings are not too many in order to avoid
hiding-places for insects, bugs, snakes and rats:
vsm1.3:99.5: even a single bed and chair only.
vsm1.3:99.6:
The right kind of inner and outer garments for him are of any superior stuff such
as China cloth, Somāra cloth, silk, fine cotton, fine linen,
vsm1.3:99.7: of either single or double thickness,
vsm1.3:99.9: and well dyed, quite pure in colour to befit an ascetic.
vsm1.3:99.10: The right kind of bowl is made of iron, as well shaped as a water bubble,
vsm1.3:99.11: as polished as a gem, spotless,
vsm1.3:99.12: and of quite pure colour to befit an ascetic.
vsm1.3:99.13: The right kind of road on which to wander for alms is free from dangers,
vsm1.3:99.15: with the village neither too far nor too near.
vsm1.3:99.16: The right kind of village in which to wander for alms is where people, thinking, “Now our lord is coming,”
vsm1.3:99.17: prepare a seat in a sprinkled, swept place,
vsm1.3:99.18: and going out to meet him, take his bowl,
vsm1.3:99.19: lead him to the house, seat him on a prepared seat
vsm1.3:99.20: and serve him carefully with their own hands.
vsm1.3:100.1: Suitable people to serve him are handsome, pleasing,
vsm1.3:100.3: scented with the perfume of incense and the smell of flowers,
vsm1.3:100.4: adorned with apparel made of variously-dyed clean pretty cloth,
vsm1.3:100.6: The right kind of gruel, rice, and hard food has colour, smell and taste,
vsm1.3:100.7: possesses nutritive essence, and is inviting,
vsm1.3:100.8: superior in every way, and enough for his wants.
vsm1.3:100.9: The right kind of posture for him is lying down or sitting.
vsm1.3:100.10: The object of his contemplation should be anyone of the colour kasiṇas, beginning with the blue, whose colour is quite pure.
vsm1.3:100.11: This is what suits one of hating temperament.
vsm1.3:101.1: The right lodging for one of deluded temperament has a view and is not shut in,
vsm1.3:101.2: where the four quarters are visible to him as he sits there.
vsm1.3:101.3: As to the postures, walking is right.
vsm1.3:101.4: The right kind of object for his contemplation is not small, that is to say,
vsm1.3:101.5: the size of a winnowing basket or the size of a saucer;
vsm1.3:101.6: for his mind becomes more confused in a confined space; so the right kind is an amply large kasiṇa.
vsm1.3:101.7: The rest is as stated for one of hating temperament. This is what suits one of deluded temperament.
vsm1.3:102.1: For one of faithful temperament all the directions given for one of hating temperament are suitable.
vsm1.3:102.2: As to the object of his contemplation, one of the recollections is right as well.
vsm1.3:102.3: For one of intelligent temperament there is nothing unsuitable as far as concerns the lodging and so on.
vsm1.3:102.4: For one of speculative temperament an open lodging with a view,
vsm1.3:102.5: where gardens, groves and ponds, pleasant prospects,
vsm1.3:102.6: panoramas of villages, towns and countryside,
vsm1.3:102.7: and the blue gleam of mountains, are visible to him as he sits there,
vsm1.3:102.9: for that is a condition for the running hither and thither of applied thought.
vsm1.3:102.10:
So he should live in a lodging such as a deep cavern screened by woods like the Overhanging
Rock of the Elephant’s Belly (Hatthikucchipabbhāra), or Mahinda’s Cave.
vsm1.3:102.11: Also an ample-sized object of contemplation is not suitable for him;
vsm1.3:102.12: for one like that is a condition for the running hither and thither of applied thought.
vsm1.3:102.14: The rest is as stated for one of greedy temperament. This is what suits one of speculative temperament.
vsm1.3:102.15:
These are the details, with definition of the kind, source, recognition, and what is suitable, as regards
the various temperaments handed down here with the words “that suits his own temperament” (§60).
vsm1.3:103.1: However, the meditation subject that is suitable to the temperament has not been cleared up in all its aspects yet.
vsm1.3:103.2: This will become clear automatically when those in the following list are treated in detail.
vsm1.3:103.3: Description of the Forty Meditation Subjects
vsm1.3:103.4: Now, it was said above, “and he should apprehend from among the forty meditation subjects one that suits his own temperament” (§60).
vsm1.3:103.5: Here the exposition of the meditation subject should be first understood in these ten ways: (1) as to enumeration,
vsm1.3:103.6: (2) as to which bring only access and which absorption,
vsm1.3:103.7: (3) as to the kinds of jhāna,
vsm1.3:104.1: 1. Herein, as to enumeration: it was said above, “from among the forty meditation subjects” (§28).
vsm1.3:104.2: Herein, the forty meditation subjects are these:
vsm1.3:105.1: Herein, the ten kasiṇas are these: earth kasiṇa, water kasiṇa, fire kasiṇa, air kasiṇa,
vsm1.3:105.2: blue kasiṇa, yellow kasiṇa, red kasiṇa, white kasiṇa,
vsm1.3:105.4: The ten kinds of foulness are these: the bloated, the livid, the festering, the cut-up, the gnawed,
vsm1.3:105.5: the scattered, the hacked and scattered, the bleeding, the worm-infested, and a skeleton.
vsm1.3:105.6:
The ten kinds of recollection are these: recollection of the Buddha (the Enlightened
One), recollection of the Dhamma (the Law), recollection of the Sangha (the Community),
vsm1.3:105.7: recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, recollection of deities,
vsm1.3:105.8: recollection (or mindfulness) of death, mindfulness occupied with the body, mindfulness of breathing, and recollection of peace.
vsm1.3:105.9: The four divine abidings are these: loving-kindness, compassion, gladness, and equanimity.
vsm1.3:105.10: The four immaterial states are these: the base consisting of boundless space, the base consisting of boundless consciousness,
vsm1.3:105.11: the base consisting of nothingness, and the base consisting of neither perception nor non-perception.
vsm1.3:105.12: The one perception is the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment.
vsm1.3:105.13: The one defining is the defining of the four elements. This is how the exposition should be understood “as to enumeration.”
vsm1.3:106.1: 2. As to which bring access only and which absorption:
vsm1.3:106.2: the eight recollections—excepting mindfulness occupied with the body and mindfulness of breathing—
vsm1.3:106.3: the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment,
vsm1.3:106.4: and the defining of the four elements,
vsm1.3:106.5: are ten meditation subjects that bring access only.
vsm1.3:106.7: This is “as to which bring access only and which absorption.”
vsm1.3:107.1: 3. As to the kind of jhāna:
vsm1.3:107.2: among those that bring absorption, the ten kasiṇas together with mindfulness of breathing bring all four jhānas.
vsm1.3:107.3: The ten kinds of foulness together with mindfulness occupied with the body bring the first jhāna.
vsm1.3:107.4: The first three divine abidings bring three jhānas.
vsm1.3:107.5: The fourth divine abiding and the four immaterial states bring the fourth jhāna. This is “as to the kind of jhāna.”
vsm1.3:108.1: 4. As to surmounting: there are two kinds of surmounting, that is to say, surmounting of factors and surmounting of object.
vsm1.3:108.2: Herein, there is surmounting of factors in the case of all meditation subjects that bring three and four jhānas
vsm1.3:108.3:
because the second jhāna, etc., have to be reached in those same objects by surmounting
the jhāna factors of applied thought and sustained thought, and so on.
vsm1.3:108.4: Likewise in the case of the fourth divine abiding;
vsm1.3:108.5: for that has to be reached by surmounting joy in the same object as that of loving-kindness, and so on.
vsm1.3:108.6: But in the case of the four immaterial states there is surmounting of the object;
vsm1.3:108.7: for the base consisting of boundless space has to be reached by surmounting one or other of the first nine kasiṇas,
vsm1.3:108.8: and the base consisting of boundless consciousness, etc., have respectively to be reached by surmounting space, and so on.
vsm1.3:108.9: With the rest there is no surmounting. This is “as to surmounting.”
vsm1.3:109.1: 5. As to extension and non-extension: only the ten kasiṇas among these forty meditation subjects need be extended.
vsm1.3:109.2: For it is within just so much space as one is intent upon with the kasiṇa
vsm1.3:109.3: that one can hear sounds with the divine ear element,
vsm1.3:109.4: see visible objects with the divine eye,
vsm1.3:109.5: and know the minds of other beings with the mind.
vsm1.3:110.1: Mindfulness occupied with the body and the ten kinds of foulness need not be extended.
vsm1.3:110.3: Because they have a definite location and because there is no benefit in it.
vsm1.3:110.4: The definiteness of their location will become clear in explaining the method of development (VIII.83–138 and VI.40, 41, 79).
vsm1.3:110.5: If the latter are extended, it is only a quantity of corpses that is extended and there is no benefit.
vsm1.3:110.6: And this is said in answer to the question of Sopāka:
vsm1.3:110.7: “Perception of visible forms is quite clear, Blessed One, perception of bones is not clear” (Source untraced);
vsm1.3:110.8: for here the perception of visible forms is called “quite clear” in the sense of extension of the sign,
vsm1.3:110.9: while the perception of bones is called “not quite clear” in the sense of its non-extension.
vsm1.3:111.1: But the words “I was intent upon this whole earth with the perception of a skeleton” (Th 18)
vsm1.3:111.2: are said of the manner of appearance to one who has acquired that perception.
vsm1.3:111.3:
For just as in the Emperor Dhammāsoka’s time the Karavīka bird uttered a sweet song when
it saw its own reflection in the looking glass walls all round
vsm1.3:111.4: and perceived Karavīkas in every direction,
vsm1.3:111.5:
so the Elder Siṅgāla Pitar thought, when he saw the sign appearing in all directions
through his acquisition of the perception of a skeleton,
vsm1.3:111.6: that the whole earth was covered with bones.
